questions.q: Which statement best reflects this course's framing of quantum machine learning (QML)?
options: QML already outperforms classical ML on most real-world business problems
QML is purely theoretical and no QML circuit can be run on real or simulated hardware today
QML has been proven to never provide any benefit, so it isn't worth studying
QML is an active research area with real theoretical interest but no proven practical advantage over classical ML today
questions.explain: The honest, accurate framing is that QML is a legitimate, active research area with real theoretical results, but no peer-reviewed, reproduced demonstration of practical advantage on real-world ML tasks exists yet.

questions.q: Why can't today's NISQ hardware simply run a large, deep variational circuit to get a more expressive model?
options: Classical computers cannot simulate any quantum circuit, so NISQ devices have no benchmark to compare against
NISQ devices have unlimited qubits but no classical control electronics
Variational circuits are only a theoretical concept and cannot run on any hardware
Deeper circuits accumulate more gate error and noise, which tends to overwhelm the signal before results become reliable
questions.explain: NISQ hardware lacks full error correction, so each additional gate/layer adds more decoherence and gate error, creating a direct tension between model expressiveness (more layers) and signal reliability (less noise).

questions.q: What is the key difference between a result being 'theoretically interesting' and 'practically advantageous' in QML, per this lesson?
options: Practically advantageous results are easier to prove than theoretically interesting ones

A theoretical speedup proof often relies on idealized assumptions (noiseless gates, efficient data loading) that don't hold for real datasets and hardware, while practical advantage requires beating the best classical approach under real-world conditions
There is no difference; any theoretical speedup automatically transfers to practical use
Theoretical interest only applies to classical algorithms, never to quantum ones
questions.explain: Proven quantum speedups frequently assume ideal, noiseless conditions and efficient data loading that aren't available in practice, which is exactly why a theoretical proof doesn't automatically mean a real, practical advantage exists.

questions.q: What does 'dequantization' refer to, as used in this lesson?
options: The process of converting a classical dataset into quantum states
Finding a classical algorithm that matches a claimed quantum speedup, removing the advantage
A hardware technique for reducing qubit decoherence
Removing noise from a quantum circuit's output using post-processing
questions.explain: Several claimed exponential QML speedups from the mid-2010s were later 'dequantized' — matched by classical algorithms — which is part of why the field is now more cautious about speedup claims.

questions.q: According to the lesson, which of these is NOT one of the three honest reasons given for learning QML despite no proven practical advantage?
options: Transferable skills — parameterized circuits and hybrid optimization loops used across variational quantum algorithms generally
QML models are already cheaper to train than classical deep learning models in production
Early positioning — being ready to verify or find a genuine advantage if one is ever discovered
Research literacy — being able to critically evaluate QML papers and vendor claims
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly avoids any claim of QML being cheaper or better in production; the three stated reasons are research literacy, transferable skills, and early positioning — none of which claim an existing practical advantage.
